https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026150024.title: Narrating ontologies of ruination in the disciplinary blur: Ruins as temporal gardens, trees as legal witnesses and birds as world-makers
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026150024.abstract: This commentary investigates the disciplinary blur that challenges the dual ontology of ruination as being both an urban/architectural transformation and an ecological phenomenon. It defies categorizations of objective knowledge and comes to terms with multispecies and interdisciplinary approaches, both historiographically and ethnographically, readjusting to the multiple temporalities of the nonhuman world-making projects that the human-made ruin becomes part of. Drawing on the urban ruin of 19 th -century Manchester (Cottonopolis), England, and the architectural ruins of contemporary Mogador, Morocco, it argues that the temporalities of the nonhuman, intersected respectively with periodicities of industrial contamination and human abandonment, transform the singular obsolete narrative of ruins into a plural transdisciplinary debate questioning the unyielding becoming of urban space. The text’s historiographical and ethnographical micronarratives, woven together through storytelling, theorize the transformative temporalities of urban nature and their capacity to provide the anthropogenic ruin with a collaborative ecological agency. This, the commentary argues, adds botanical and ornithological ontologies to urban and architectural taxonomies of ruination. By positioning oneself in the disciplinary blur, the commentary ideates on how architectural and urban studies can accommodate unfamiliar rhythms of nonhuman-constructed botanical and ornithological ruins.

https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026150000.title: Cultural buffering in entrepreneurial city diplomacy: Wuxi’s economic engagement abroad
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026150000.abstract: Why do investment-oriented municipal delegations begin with culture? This article develops cultural buffering to explain how municipal actors use cultural forms and assets when development-oriented diplomacy brings together organisations with different authority, timetables and commitments. The analysis draws on multi-sited ethnography of 5 Wuxi delegation circuits across Japan, the United Kingdom and continental Europe, followed by tracing of 21 initiatives to July 2026. It identifies two recurrent problems: municipal schedules can outrun partner learning and due diligence, while demands for visible outputs can exceed commitment and post-event ownership. Municipal actors respond to these temporal and accountability mismatches through naming, sequencing, coalition broadening and managed ambiguity. These moves can change who participates, what becomes discussable, which organisations enter the relationship and how provisional alignment is recorded. Subsequent project implementation depends on authority, resources, delivery capacity and an organisation willing to own the next step. Cultural buffering therefore identifies the encounter-level work through which an unsettled proposal becomes discussable and revisitable before its implementation is determined.

https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149809.title: Bridging critical knowledge and action gaps in urban health: A call for transdisciplinary approaches in urban studies in the era of global population aging and climate change
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149809.authors: Vitor Pessoa Colombo, Elis Borde, Mirko Severin Winkler et al.
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149809.abstract: Urbanization and population aging are two “mega-trends” posing significant challenges to global health, particularly under climate change. Despite extensive evidence on the links between the built environment and health, urban planning scholars and practitioners still miss valuable opportunities to contribute to public health and urban health equity—which often remain marginal or only implicit topics in urban planning discourses and practices. Against this background, we organized the transdisciplinary workshop “Global Health Challenges Related to Demographic & Climate Changes: Implications for Urban and Territorial Planning” (Basel, 2024), convening scholars and practitioners to co-develop a research agenda addressing knowledge-to-action gaps in urban health equity and climate resilience. Building on the workshop’s discussions, this commentary highlights current challenges in reconnecting urban planning and public health while presenting opportunities to bridge this gap. We argue for an “ultra-local” approach that acknowledges the chronic lack of granular data necessary to address spatial justice and urban health inequities, emphasizing the importance of evidence- and place-based planning. To illustrate this approach, we present two recent experiences: the BH-Viva project in Brazil, which assessed impact of slum-upgrading projects on urban health equity, and the Saint-Louis Master Plan in Senegal, a pioneering effort integrating climate resilience into urban policy and planning. Ultimately, we present what we identified as priority research paths in urban studies, having transdisciplinarity as a precondition for urban planners to effectively tackle pressing global health challenges.

https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149809.title: Interpreting mobility reform through care: Ambivalent authority in Taiwan
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149809.abstract: This article examines how human-centred mobility reform can reproduce, rather than displace, entrenched hierarchies of automobility. Focusing on Taiwan, it analyses a regulatory archive of national traffic legislation and Taipei municipal instruments through which recent safety reforms have been articulated in the language of care, participation, and protection for vulnerable road users. The article argues that these reforms do not simply replace vehicle-centred urban order with pedestrian-oriented governance. Instead, they overlay existing mobility hierarchies with increasingly dense classifications, conditional provisions, and delegated discretion. Drawing on Homi Bhabha’s concept of ambivalence, the paper conceptualises this condition as ambivalent authority: a mode of postcolonial governance in which authority must appear protective and non-coercive while preserving inherited infrastructures of motorised priority. Through analysis of human-oriented road design, pedestrian-priority legislation, scooter and non-motorised classifications, and municipal mechanisms for temporary road use, the paper shows how care becomes a territorial technology of rule. Its contribution is threefold: it links postcolonial theory to urban mobility governance, clarifies how automobility persists through reform rather than only through resistance to reform, and reframes regulatory complexity as a political mechanism through which contradictory urban priorities are managed. The article concludes that mobility reform in Taiwan governs not by resolving the tension between care and hierarchy, but by continually recalibrating it.

https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149288.title: Understanding activity spaces: Contemporary issues and challenges and future research directions
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149288.authors: Renee Zahnow, Jonathan Corcoran, Rebecca L. Wickes
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149288.abstract: Activity spaces are a subset of locations where people spend their everyday lives. Interest in activity spaces spans the social sciences, geography, health sciences and transportation research. In recent years, the spread of smartphones and other tracking devices has made it far easier to record daily movements. This has sparked an increase in activity space research and an opportunity to consider how the concept has been conceptually and empirically defined over time and across disciplinary fields. In this scoping review, we analyse 372 studies of activity spaces published between 1972 and 2024. Despite conceptual consistency, we find that studies tend to focus, empirically, on one of four dimensions of activity spaces: access, nodes, paths and exposure. Drawing on our review, we suggest greater methodological harmonisation may better support replication and comparative studies and incremental research discovery. We propose that to achieve this, a more nuanced theoretical framework is required that defines each of the dimensions of activity space, how they are related to each other and incorporates aspects of daily activity in the new millennia (e.g. online, hybrid and multilayered time–space locations).

https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149868.title: Build for whom? Contested state entrepreneurialism and the governance of affordable rental housing in Shanghai, China
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149868.abstract: This paper critically interrogates state entrepreneurialism through an empirical analysis of China’s recent Affordable Rental Housing (ARH) programme. Prevailing accounts of social housing under neoliberalism tend to frame it as a residual, market-enabling instrument of welfare retrenchment. Such perspectives, however, inadequately capture contexts in which expanded provision is intertwined with intensified and reconfigured forms of state intervention. Drawing on 92 qualitative interviews in Shanghai, this paper shows how ARH operates as a strategically selective mechanism embedded within broader projects of labour governance and territorial development. While it functions as a spatial fix to absorb oversupplied housing stock amid the crisis tendencies of land-centred accumulation, its implementation reveals a fragmented and contested process of state entrepreneurialism. Intra-state frictions, bureaucratic negotiations and divergent local growth rationalities reproduce uneven and contingent outcomes, rather than a coherent developmental logic. Access to ARH is selectively structured to privilege skilled migrants, demonstrating how state housing provision is mobilised to sort labour and align welfare responsibilities with labour value extraction and urban competitiveness. Meanwhile, hierarchical state-market arrangements reproduce regulatory asymmetries and uneven access. This paper argues that social housing in contemporary China constitutes a contested terrain of accumulation and legitimation, complicating linear narratives of neoliberal convergence and advancing a more critical understanding of state-led housing provision.

https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149868.title: Beyond the perimeter walls: Negotiated porosity and the governance of megaproject edges in Metro Manila
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149868.abstract: This article examines Bonifacio Global City (BGC), an urban megaproject in Metro Manila, from the perspective of two adjacent barangays, or local government units: Guadalupe Nuevo and South Cembo. Drawing on fieldwork conducted between 2017 and 2024, it asks how these barangays manage the demands of a megaproject planned and marketed as self-contained, and how interdependence at the enclave edge becomes a basis for contesting the terms of urban porosity. Like many central business districts, BGC does not house many of the workers its economy depends on; it relies in part on adjacent barangays that provide the lower-cost housing, everyday services and mobility connections many workers require. The closure and later negotiated reopening of the J.P. Rizal butas, a long-standing informal opening in BGC’s perimeter wall, made this interdependence politically visible. From this case, the paper develops the concept of negotiated porosity. The term describes how the dependencies that sustain an enclave can become spatially concentrated at an interruptible point on its edge, allowing local government actors to contest the status and terms of access across the boundary. The article contributes to work on enclave urbanism, porous enclaves and the governance of urban megaprojects in the Philippines and beyond.

https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026147354.title: From Frankenstein to Gulliver urbanism: Reframing AI and scale in urban theory
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026147354.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in urban governance, infrastructure and design, yet urban theory still lacks a clear language for analysing the scale asymmetries through which these systems operate. This article develops Gulliver Urbanism as a conceptual framework for understanding how AI reshapes urban power when it processes information, acts, and coordinates across cognitive, temporal and spatial horizons that exceed ordinary human capacities and institutional rhythms. Moving beyond Frankenstein Urbanism’s emphasis on rebellion and loss of control, we argue that the central problem of contemporary AI urbanism is scale asymmetry within co-constituted human and machine assemblages. The framework comprises six dimensions: cognitive scale, temporal scale, spatial scale, governance asymmetry, autonomy and agency and human response. It synthesises scholarship on AI urbanism, urban political economy, infrastructural urbanism, posthumanism, law and scale, supported by AI governance frameworks and vignettes on Hangzhou City Brain, robotaxis and generative design. The article conceptualises the urban as a constitutive condition of AI scale asymmetry, where algorithmic systems encounter infrastructure, land, mobility, public services, municipal authority, social difference and collective life. Across these domains, the key challenge is how to govern systems whose capacities outpace human oversight while remaining embedded in corporate, legal and political arrangements. We argue that effective responses require mixed-intelligence governance and temporal dignity: arrangements that subject algorithmic operations to democratic oversight, contestation and human-paced deliberation. Gulliver Urbanism explains how AI reconstitutes urban life by reorganising infrastructures, municipal authority, spatial relations, design imaginaries, public services and everyday citizenship.

https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149813.title: Internationalization of progressive municipalism—Barcelona international relations strategies
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149813.abstract: This article examines how the International Relations Master Plan 2020–2023 and the International Strategy 2025–2029 translate progressive municipalism into external action. Through qualitative content analysis and comparison, it identifies three mechanisms of internationalization: norm projection, networked amplification, and multilevel resource mobilization. Both Strategies promote a rights-based agenda centered on social justice, housing, democratic participation, digital rights, and ecological transition. However, the movement-oriented municipalism of the Colau administration has evolved under Collboni into a more institutionalized and partnership-based model. This shift demonstrates both the continuity and moderation of Barcelona’s progressive orientation. The article also highlights the limits of municipal internationalization: although the Strategies support agenda-setting, policy circulation, coalition-building, and access to resources, they neither confer formal international authority on the city nor guarantee implementation. Barcelona, therefore, illustrates both the potential and the structural constraints of cities seeking to influence state-centered international governance.

https://doi.org/10.1007/s11069-026-08459.title: Rockfall risk management on transportation corridors: coupling risk assessment with terrestrial mobile LiDAR survey on the A22 motorway (South Tyrol, Italy)
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11069-026-08459.authors: Francesco Lelli, Diana Bianchi, Vincenzo Critelli et al.
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11069-026-08459.abstract: Abstract This study presents an integrated approach, coupling rockfall risk assessment with a vehicle-based surveying for the large-scale management of slope assets along transportation corridors. Rockfall risk was assessed qualitatively using relative rating scales. To reduce the subjectivity inherent in expert judgment, susceptibility was estimated through probabilistic methods, while vulnerability was informed by conventional runout simulations. Despite the associated uncertainties, the occurrence of a January 2024 rockfall within an area classified as high risk provides independent qualitative support for the consistency of the first-level screening results. Terrestrial Mobile LiDAR (TML) survey conducted from a car was designed to maximise effectiveness and efficiency in capturing rockfall-prone slopes and establishing a baseline for long-term monitoring. Its actual effectiveness, efficiency, potential and limitations were evaluated through a survey conducted in April 2023. Approximately 3.5 km of the A22 motorway, representing more than one-quarter of the analysed section, were found to be potentially exposed to rockfall risk, originating from 27 of the 55 identified potential detachment zones. The TML survey successfully detected over 70% of these zones, achieving a point density potentially sufficient to identify volumes greater than approximately 10 dm 3 . The scanning was constrained by morphological conditions, such as vertical slopes adjacent to the motorway, structural obstacles, such as tunnel portals, and the instrument’s maximum range of 475 m. Despite these limitations, the quality and accuracy of the acquired data indicate that the TML can effectively support the motorway operators in large-scale rockfall risk management.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebc9e.title: Decomposing drivers of global temperature change after net zero
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebc9e.authors: Annika Högner, Zebedee Nicholls, Gaurav Ganti
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebc9e.abstract: Abstract Net-zero CO2 (NZCO2) and greenhouse gas emission (GHG) targets are central to the development of mitigation scenarios. Projected global surface air temperature (GSAT) change after NZCO2 depends on several factors that broadly fall into two categories: scenario-specific factors that account for the diversity of possible mitigation pathways to net zero and beyond, and model-specific factors that describe the climate system response, captured in the zero emissions commitment (ZEC). Current established climate assessment approaches do not separate contributions from these two categories to post-net-zero GSAT change in GHG emission scenarios. To address this shortcoming, we propose a diagnostic protocol that decomposes the contributions from the model-specific ZEC and from key scenario-characteristics including non-CO2 GHG reductions, net-negative CO2 emissions, and other climate forcers. We assess the GSAT outcomes from a large collection of scenarios that achieve NZCO2 using the MAGICC model. We find a peak warming increase of 0.08°C (‘likely (>66%)’ 0.05 to 0.11°C) per decade delay in reaching NZCO2 and a -0.11°C (likely -0.13 to -0.05°C) post-NZCO2 GSAT decline by 2100. Based on our decomposition approach we find that the model-specific negative ZEC contributes about -0.03°C across the full scenario set. This is on the same order as the contribution from non-CO2 mitigation for scenarios that achieve NZGHG. The decomposition allows us to test the sensitivity of our outcomes. We apply the IPCC AR6 WGI assessed value of 0°C (likely ±0.19°C) for ZEC and find that the median likelihood of no further warming on multidecadal timescales after achieving and maintaining NZCO2 drops from just about 85% to 67%. After achieving and maintaining NZGHG, however, it remains ‘very likely (>90%)’. This underlines the need for setting preventive mitigation targets to account for potential stronger than expected Earth system feedbacks and demonstrates the utility of a decomposition approach.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebc9f.title: Terrestrial protected areas are not effective in mitigating human pressure on biodiversity
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebc9f.authors: Katharina Ramm, Calum Brown, Almut Arneth, Mark Rounsevell
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebc9f.abstract: Abstract Global biodiversity is declining rapidly and protected areas are a major conservation measure aiming to reverse this negative trend by limiting pressures on biodiversity in particular locations. There are increasing calls to protect larger areas, but also growing evidence that an increase in area alone is insufficient. At least as important is the effectiveness of existing and new protected areas. We apply a novel biodiversity pressure index that encompasses the five direct drivers of biodiversity loss identified by IPBES to analyse pressures in protected areas globally. We use a GLMM to assess which variables shape the pressure levels within protected areas. We find that there are still notable human pressures in protected areas globally. Strict protection and larger size of protected areas result in lower pressures, while high national-level corruption levels result in higher pressures. The results confirm that an increase in the number of protected areas will not necessarily conserve biodiversity effectively, unless they achieve greater control of the underlying drivers of biodiversity loss, including spatially diffuse pressures and those that currently compromise small protected areas in countries with unstable governance.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aeb4c8.title: Food redistribution: a critical review of an overlooked priority measure against food waste
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aeb4c8.authors: Zhang, C., Zhu, F., Song, Y., Ji, Y. et al.
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aeb4c8.abstract: Abstract Food redistribution is widely recognized as a preferred strategy for reducing food loss and waste. Yet it is still treated mainly as charitable relief, while its broader role in governance and the conditions for effective implementation remain insufficiently articulated. Drawing on a triple bottom line perspective and sustainable development goal coupling framework, this study synthesizes evidence from the literature, international practice, and field research in China to examine the contributions of food redistribution, the constraints that shape its performance, and the models through which it can be scaled. We find that existing research provides much stronger evidence on social benefits than on economic mechanisms or environmental outcomes, which remain constrained by value-cost mismatches, uncertainty in substitution assumptions, and limited activity data. Cross-dimensional evaluation and analysis of synergies also remain weak. In practice, international experience points to a transferable operational architecture based on hub-and-spoke networks and standardized procedures, but successful scaling depends on aligning policy tools with operational mechanisms to reduce systemic frictions. The Chinese cases extend this understanding by identifying two complementary implementation models, centralized and decentralized, each adapted to different institutional and market conditions. Together, these findings highlight the important role of food redistribution in sustainable food and waste governance, and offer practical support for integrated evaluation and wider implementation.

https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-026-04328.title: Attribution science and climate change litigation in India
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-026-04328.abstract: Abstract In climate change litigation, attribution science is increasingly being used as an evidentiary tool to ascertain responsibility, accountability, liability, and provide redress the impact on human life and the environment. The Indian judiciary implicitly uses scientific evidence in an unstructured or fragmented manner without it being clearly labelled as attribution science. This current ad-hoc reliance on scientific evidence without an identifiable scale may lead to inconsistencies in judicial outcomes, undermine legal certainty, and hinder the transparent and systematic development of climate jurisprudence. Drawing on the mathematical work of Charles Weiss, we offer an interdisciplinary explanatory climate framework that addresses the uncertainty of science by assembling a scale of legal standards arranged in a hierarchy of levels of increasing certainty familiar to the judiciary and lawyers. The originality of this article lies in extending Charles Weiss ‘standard-of-proof’ scale to address how attribution science integrates within a calibrated language of confidence and likelihood, terms used in the IPCC’s framework (Sixth Assessment Report). Reported Indian cases from the Supreme Court, High Courts and the National Green Tribunal are selected to illustrate levels of scientific certainty or uncertainty and corresponding legal standards of proof constituting acceptable bases for legal decisions in climate change litigation. The adoption of a ‘scientifically legal’ climate lexicon helps increase the precision and rationality regarding the different threshold levels for establishing causation. This article encourages next step thinking within the climate attribution adjudicative process thereby developing context-specific benchmarks that reflect India’s constitutional safeguards, precautionary ethos, and public-interest litigation traditions.

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.buildenv.2026..title: Morphology-based classification and error-controlled reduction of urban weather files with Torino as a case study
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.buildenv.2026..abstract: Urban morphology creates intra-urban thermal variability that a single airport EnergyPlus Weather (EPW) file cannot represent. This study develops a reproducible GIS-to-Urban Weather Generator (UWG) framework for Torino, Italy, separating morphological classification from weather-product reduction. A preliminary building-seeded cell method was audited before adopting 100 m assignment cells characterised through overlapping 500 × 500 m neighbourhood supports. Support-size (250–1000 m) and 50 m grid-shift sensitivities were tested. Building fraction, area-weighted height, facade-to-site ratio, tree cover, and grass cover were extracted for 12,997 locations; 10,593 quality-screened supports were classified using robust scaling and CLARA-style k-medoids. Seven morphology classes balanced interpretability and spatial coherence, although four ranked best statistically, and classification robustness was moderate. Under a common UWG template, four representative EPWs were retained by curve inspection and minimax selection, with a 0.10°C maximum-error screen and a diminishing-return criterion. Maximum medoid hourly dry-bulb RMSE was 0.06°C with the delivered one-decimal EPWs and 0.04°C at diagnostic three-decimal serialisation. Across 105 stratified non-medoid supports, weighted mean and 95th-percentile RMSE were 0.05 and 0.10°C, but a 1.33°C industrial-tail error required a conservative post hoc restriction, not a validated applicability boundary. Synchronised processed 2022 station comparisons improved annual RMSE relative to Caselle only at Consolata. Humidity limitations preclude interpreting temperature fidelity as complete EPW validation. The atlas links coordinates to morphology classes, UWG configurations, and candidate EPWs. The restricted library distinguishes simulator-conditional reduction fidelity from observational accuracy.

https://doi.org/10.1080/00038628.2026.27.abstract: Age-related declines in navigation can limit mobility and independence. Although wayfinding guidelines often emphasize landmarks, older adults increasingly rely on route-based strategies. To address this gap, we tested whether pathway configuration could support route learning and consequently improve wayfinding. Using immersive virtual reality, 76 younger (20–34 years) and 52 older (58–80 years) adults explored an environment with either a grid-shaped or star-shaped pathway layout. In the star layout, each destination was reached via a specific route, potentially strengthening route-target associations. Older adults generally travelled longer paths and showed greater distance errors. However, both age groups demonstrated better navigational memory in the star layout, reflected in smaller distance errors. This advantage was not explained by longer paths during initial exploration. Our findings suggest that pathway configuration can support route-based navigation across adulthood and highlight the potential of architectural design to improve wayfinding in public spaces.

https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-026-04339.title: Reconstruction of extreme temperature events in medieval Poland (1001–1500 CE) from documentary evidence
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-026-04339.authors: Akbari Moghaddam Sani, S., Przybylak, R., Oliński, P.
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-026-04339.abstract: Abstract Understanding the frequency, intensity, and societal impacts of extreme weather is essential for reconstructing past climate variability, yet systematic documentary-based reconstructions remain remarkably limited for medieval Poland. To address this gap in pre-instrumental data, this study reconstructs extreme temperature-related weather and climate events in Poland between 1001 and 1500 CE utilizing historical documentary evidence. A total of 299 extreme events were verified and synthesized from 452 primary weather notes. To mitigate duplication, overlapping accounts of the same anomaly were cross-referenced and merged. Validated events were categorized into severe frost; cold waves; river, lake, and sea ice events; snow and snowstorms; and heat and warm waves, with each classified by intensity, duration, and source reliability. The findings reveal a clear dominance of cold-related extremes, particularly severe frost and cold waves. A significant increase in the frequency and clustering of these events is observed during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, peaking specifically in the 1440s and 1450s. This pattern aligns with the broader Central European transition into the early phase of the Little Ice Age. Spatial analysis indicates a concentration of recorded events in the Baltic Coast, Pomerania, and Silesia, though this partly reflects uneven source preservation in prominent historical economic centers. Furthermore, cold extremes heavily disrupted transportation and caused environmental stress, whereas heat waves were strongly associated with agricultural damage. By integrating documentary evidence with quantitative analysis, this database provides crucial insights into historical climate variability and climate-society interactions.

https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-026-02488.title: Complex lake effects structure bryophyte communities across spatial scales around Lake Superior, Canada
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-026-02488.authors: Varina E. Crisfield, D. Holt-Schmitt, Valentinà Buttò, Nicole J. Fenton
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-026-02488.abstract: Studies have found that large lakes significantly modify regional climates, an influence known as the “lake effect”. Large lakes may provide biodiversity refugia in a changing climate owing to the lake effect, but the impacts of lake effects on biodiversity remain poorly documented. We sought to quantify the influence of the lake effect on bryophyte communities in the vicinity of Lake Superior, and to disentangle the lake effect from processes occurring at larger (regional) and smaller (forest stand) scales. We sampled bryophyte communities on three substrates (trees, rocks, and logs) across 54 sites on and near the northern and eastern shores of Lake Superior. We combined community data with climate and forest data to determine the influence of variables at each of three spatial scales—micro (forest attributes), meso (lake effect), and macro (regional climatic norms)—on community composition and richness. The lake effect structured community composition, along with regional climate norms and forest characteristics. The lake effect was divided into three orthogonal axes. Notably, each of these axes included a distinct component of the moisture environment—precipitation, relative humidity, and vapour pressure deficit—and our results suggest that these components have divergent effects on bryophyte communities. The lake effect had no significant influence on species richness. Lake Superior induces biotically important climatic heterogeneity that structures bryophyte communities across the study region. The near-lake environment may be an important thermal and hydrologic refuge for bryophytes in a warming, drying climate.

https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-026-02795.title: Declining environmental predictability erodes reproduction in a tropical seabird
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-026-02795.authors: Santiago Ortega, Cristina Rodríguez, Ayumi Mizuno et al.
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-026-02795.abstract: Seasonal breeders often depend on predictable resource pulses, yet climate change may alter reliability without shifting average timing. Here, using satellite chlorophyll records and two decades of individual breeding data for a tropical seabird, we show that weakened breeding synchrony and declining and less consistent reproductive success were associated with increasingly variable bloom timing without a consistent directional shift. Focusing on average timing alone could mean that climate impacts on species are overlooked. The authors show that, for a tropical seabird model species, winter–spring phytoplankton blooms kept a stable mean timing but became more variable between years. Breeding synchrony weakened and reproductive success declined and became less consistent over the same two decades.

https://doi.org/10.1007/s11069-026-08454.title: Short-term shallow landslide early warning framework integrating radar-based precipitation forecasts and a physically based slope stability model in Taiwan
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11069-026-08454.authors: Jui-Yi Ho, Chung-Yi Lin, Che-Hsin Liu et al.
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11069-026-08454.abstract: Abstract Taiwan is prone to hillslope disasters in mountain areas because of its special topographical, geological, and hydrological conditions. During typhoons and rainstorms, severe shallow landslides frequently occur. To mitigate the impact of shallow landslides, not only the structural measures are necessary, but also adequate warning systems and contingency measures must be executed. Hence, precise precipitation forecasts and landslide prediction are the most important measures in practice. To account for inherent weather uncertainties precipitation forecasts based on quantitative precipitation forecast model with radar data assimilation method and ensemble mean prediction were adopted in this study instead of using a single model output. The SIMTOP model based on infinite-slope model and TOPMODEL was developed. In considering detail topographic characteristics of the subcatchments, the proposed model can estimate the variation of saturated water level during rainstorms, and then link with the slope instability analysis to clarify whether shallow landslides would occur in the subcatchment. Two area vulnerable to landslide in Taiwan were collected to test the applicability of the model for landslide prediction. Six typhoons events were used to verify the applicability of the proposed model. Four indexes including the probability of detection (POD), false alarm ratio (FAR), threat score (TS), and accuracy (ACC) were adopted to assess the performance of two kinds of very short-term rainfall forecasts with SIMTOP model. The results indicate that quantitative precipitation forecast model with radar data assimilation with SIMTOP model was better than ensemble rainfall forecasts with SIMTOP model. It is promising to apply the proposed model for landslide early warnings to reduce the magnitude of the loss of lives and properties.

https://doi.org/10.1007/s11069-026-08501.title: Landslide susceptibility mapping through the integration of pixel and slope unit analyses: a case study in El Salvador, Central America
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11069-026-08501.authors: Christian Conoscenti, Abel Alexei Argueta-Platero, Liborio Barbera et al.
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11069-026-08501.abstract: Abstract Landslide susceptibility mapping is commonly performed using either pixel-based or slope-unit (SU)-based approaches, each characterised by specific advantages and limitations. In this study, SU-level information is incorporated directly into a pixel-based modelling framework to assess whether this integration improves model performance and the spatial organisation of susceptibility maps. The analysis focuses on the northern sector of the Ilopango Caldera (El Salvador), where shallow landslides were triggered by Tropical Storms Amanda and Cristobal in 2020. A 2 m resolution LiDAR-derived DEM was used to derive pixel-scale terrain predictors and to delineate slope units through hydrological analysis. Two configurations were tested: a Baseline model based solely on pixel-scale variables and an Enhanced model including SU-based morphometric summaries and lithological proportions. Both configurations were implemented using Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS) and Random Forest (RF) and evaluated through repeated spatial cross-validation. The Enhanced models systematically outperformed the Baseline models. Mean AUC increased from 0.927 to 0.942 for MARS and from 0.923 to 0.949 for RF. In addition to the improvement in predictive performance, the Enhanced configuration produced maps characterised by higher spatial autocorrelation, measured using Global Moran’s I, and reduced local fragmentation, while maintaining variability within individual slope units. These results indicate that integrating SU-derived descriptors during model calibration strengthens the predictive capability of pixel-based models and improves the spatial consistency of the resulting maps, without sacrificing pixel-scale detail.

https://link.springer.com/article/10.100.title: Short-term shallow landslide early warning framework integrating radar-based precipitation forecasts and a physically based slope stability model in Taiwan
https://link.springer.com/article/10.100.abstract: Shallow landslides are among the most frequent rainfall-induced hazards in Taiwan’s mountainous regions, particularly during typhoon events when rainfall intensity changes rapidly over short periods. Reliable very short-term rainfall forecast is therefore essential for enhancing near-real-time landslide early warning. This study develops an integrated framework that couples two quantitative precipitation forecast (QPF) approaches—radar data assimilation and ensemble mean forecasts—with the physically based SIMTOP slope stability model. Six typhoon events associated with documented shallow landslides were selected to evaluate the forecasting skill and warning performance of the combined system. The rainfall forecast assessment showed that both QPF methods performed reasonably well for 1–3 h lead times but deteriorated beyond 4 h. Radar-assimilated forecasts consistently provided more accurate representations of rainfall evolution than ensemble means, particularly in capturing peak intensities. When incorporated into SIMTOP, the radar-based QPF produced stronger short-term landslide predictions, achieving POD, FAR, TS, and ACC values of 0.813, 0.480, 0.464, and 0.979, respectively, for 1–4 h forecasts. Performance declined at 5–6 h due to increasing uncertainty, whereas the ensemble mean forecasts displayed generally weaker skill across all lead times. Overall, the results indicate that integrating radar-enhanced precipitation forecasts with a physically based slope stability model can substantially improve the timeliness and reliability of shallow landslide warnings under typhoon rainfall. The proposed framework provides a practical tool for supporting rapid emergency response and for strengthening disaster risk reduction efforts in landslide-prone mountain areas.

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijdrr.2026.106.title: Geo-social media beyond Twitter: Comparing retrieval strategies for Reddit, TikTok, Telegram, Mastodon, and Bluesky during the 2024 Central European floods
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijdrr.2026.106.authors: Shaily Raju Gandhi, Marco Badici, David Hanny et al.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijdrr.2026.106.abstract: Social media can provide timely information during floods, but cross-platform keyword retrieval remains challenging because search interfaces and access conditions differ. This study retrospectively compared English- and German-language posts retrieved from Bluesky, Mastodon, Reddit, TikTok and Telegram during the September 2024 Central European floods. Two strategies - phrase-based queries (Test 1) and root-based, stem-like queries (Test 2) - were applied using equivalent keyword sets adapted to each platform’s constraints. Performance was evaluated in terms of retrieval volume, duplication, disaster relatedness, relevance and geoparsed location references. Spatial patterns were analysed through H3 aggregation and spatial autocorrelation and validated against a satellite-derived flood mask. Bluesky and TikTok yielded the largest volumes (11,232 versus 49,386 posts and 9718 versus 25,560 posts, respectively, for Tests 1 and 2), whereas Reddit (246 versus 249) and Telegram (85 versus 83) had substantially fewer posts. Root-based queries substantially increased retrieval volume on Bluesky, Mastodon and TikTok, but phrase-based queries produced a higher proportion of relevant content. About one third of geocoded related-and-relevant posts (33.1% and 34.4%) were geoparsed to the United States, showing that global retrieval captures international discourse alongside local observations; spatial analyses were therefore restricted to Central Europe. At H3 Level 4, 83.81% of occupied cells under Test 1 and 81.82% under Test 2 intersected the flood mask, exceeding the 67.73% spatial baseline. Cells containing posts from multiple platforms represented 40.00% and 36.36% of the respective spatial footprints. Multi-platform integration increased overall spatial completeness and reduced the likelihood of platform-specific blind spots.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f2.title: Effects of high elevation wildfires on peak snow water equivalent in California's Sierra Nevada headwater regions
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f2.authors: Xiaoyu Liang, Yufang Jin, Kyle  R. Knipper et al.
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f2.abstract: Abstract Increases in high‐elevation wildfires in California’s Sierra Nevada region (SNR) have raised concerns about potential impacts on snowpack, a major source for the state’s water supply. Quantifying fire-induced changes in snow storage remains challenging in mountainous regions with complex topography and large climatic and ecological gradients, due to limited field observations and process models. This study leveraged high-resolution Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) lidar surveys (2023-2024) to assess the impacts of 2020-2021 wildfires on peak snow water equivalent (SWE) across six SNR watersheds. We assembled >32,000 matched burned-unburned 50-m pixel pairs with similar pre-fire environmental conditions and assessed how changes in peak SWE (ΔpeakSWE: burned - unburned) varied with burn severity, pre-fire forest structure, meteorological variables, and terrain above the snowline. Across matched pairs, post-fire peak SWE differences varied in both magnitude and direction, depending on yearly weather (e.g., wet vs. normal year) and local environmental setting. The largest positive burned–unburned difference occurred in dense forests with ≥75% canopy loss at intermediate elevations in 2023, where burned areas had 13.0 cm higher peak SWE on average (12% relative to the matched unburned mean of 105.1 cm); this difference was substantially smaller in 2024. The spatially cross-validated extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) machine learning model showed terrain provided the strongest predictive information, followed by vegetation structure. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and a shallow decision tree further showed that sites with lower heat exposure, locally lower terrain positions, and intermediate elevations generally were associated with higher peak SWE in burned areas compared to matched unburned areas, whereas taller pre-fire canopies and exposed, high-energy terrain were associated with lower peak SWE. These results demonstrate wildfire effects on peak SWE are strongly context dependent and provide an assessment framework for anticipating where high elevation wildfires may increase or reduce mountain snow storage.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f5.title: Land-use input choice and policy-relevant environmental and sustainability indicators: a sensitivity assessment for Brazil
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f5.authors: Chiara Colesanti Senni, Justin A. Johnson
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f5.abstract: Abstract Global assessments of climate, biodiversity, and ecosystem services rely on projections of land-use change (LUC), typically from integrated assessment models (IAMs) at coarse resolution (25 to 50 km) and downscaled to the 30 to 300 m required by biophysical models. The choice of LUC projection introduces large variation in results, but this variation is rarely assessed. For Brazil, we systematically compare two LUC projections, a regionally calibrated model (Land Use and Cover Change Modelling Environment, LuccME) and a global product (Land-Use Harmonization 2, LUH2), downscaling both to 300 m with the Spatial Economic Allocation Landscape Simulator (SEALS) and computing five sustainability indicators (biomass carbon, biodiversity intactness, water yield, Forest Code compliance, and a diffuse-nitrogen index). The differences are large, from −37 to +45 % for biomass carbon, −20 to +23 % for water yield, −76 to +12 % for the diffuse-nitrogen index, and −0.27 to +0.17 in mean species abundance. The choice between the two projections also flips the Forest Code compliance call on 9 to 26 % of Brazil's land grid cells, and several biome-level shifts reverse sign under an alternative class correspondence, a sensitivity we quantify. Differences of this size could materially affect sustainability analyses, including REDD+ accounting, where a shifted carbon baseline could change results-based payments, as well as biodiversity assessment and nature-related financial-risk analysis.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f1.title: Low snow fractions increase evapotranspiration efficiency across the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f1.authors: Sarah K. Newcomb, Robert Van Kirk, Sarah E. Godsey, Otto Lang
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f1.abstract: Abstract Globally, mountainous headwaters are projected to experience less precipitation falling as snow. Changes in snowmelt rate and timing may affect streamflow generation by shifting the alignment of energy and water inputs which control the proportion of precipitation lost to the atmosphere, or evapotranspiration (ET) efficiency. Since changes in ET efficiency may make streamflow harder to predict in seasonally snow-covered watersheds, in this study, we investigate the impact of precipitation phase on ET efficiency in eight watersheds across the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. ET efficiency has significantly increased in four watersheds with greater land cover change (p < 0.05). Across all watersheds, mixed effects modeling shows that more available water goes to ET in low snow-fraction years. However, ET responses to snow conditions are locally moderated: groundwater-dominated watersheds are less responsive in the short term but retain a stronger memory of the previous year's conditions. These findings indicate vegetation water use and ET will more strongly affect streamflow generation in seasonally snow-covered regions during low snow years, potentially exacerbating existing droughts

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f0.title: Interdecadal Pacific variability modulates recent drying and near-term changes in early-spring precipitation over subtropical East Asia
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f0.authors: Zejiang Yin, Zhang Lei, Song Yang et al.
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f0.abstract: Abstract Subtropical East Asia, among the world's most densely populated regions and a major agricultural region, has experienced pronounced early-spring drying since the 1980s, posing growing risks to water resources and agriculture. However, the relative contributions of external forcing and internal variability to the drying trend, as well as the associated dynamic and thermodynamic processes, remain unclear. The circulation analogues-based dynamic adjustment reveals that atmospheric circulation changes explain approximately 108% of the observed drying trend, which were largely driven by internal variability. These circulation changes are closely linked to a positive-to-negative phase transition of the Interdecadal Pacific Variability (IPV), which can suppress precipitation by weakening the Northwest Pacific anticyclone and inducing anomalous subsidence over subtropical East Asia. The IPV also modulates near-term precipitation projections. Based on the projected IPV inferred from ensemble members that realistically capture the historical IPV, we identify a likely reversal toward wetter conditions in the near future.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f4.title: Identifying the indirect cost of work in high-heat conditions
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f4.authors: Steven C. Sherwood, Timothy L. Neal, Ollie Jay
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec1f4.abstract: Abstract The impact of excess heat on labor productivity and/or labor supply are a key contributor to the total economic impact of climate change on the macroeconomy. Previous studies do not adequately distinguish between the short run labor response to excess heat and indirect costs to health and well being, or quantify the additional indirect toll of extreme heat. Empirically, workers typically exceed international safety standard work hours under hot conditions, suggesting they are incurring indirect costs in order to reduce production losses. Here we take a simple agent-based perspective on this question, supposing that workers and their employers make this tradeoff optimally. Based on this and a few other simple assumptions we infer workplace heat impacts on human health and well being that may be an appreciable fraction of economic losses. This implies that current studies underestimate the true costs of workplace heat in the present, and especially, future climates.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aeb70c.title: Who collects, who purchases? Land ownership and biomass acquisition in LMICs
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aeb70c.authors: Dim, J., Lopez Soto, D., Balasubramanya, S., Kumar, P.
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aeb70c.abstract: Abstract This study examines the relationship between agricultural land ownership and household fuel use behavior in low- and middle-income countries. Using harmonized household survey data from 11 countries and pooled regressions with country fixed effects, the analysis compares land-owning and landless households across three dimensions of fuel behavior: firewood collection, firewood purchase, and firewood use as the main cooking fuel. The results show that land-owning households are more likely to collect firewood, less likely to purchase it, and more likely to rely on firewood as their primary cooking fuel. These findings persist after controlling for wealth, urban residence, electricity access, and household composition. Interaction models indicate that the land–collection relationship is stable across varying contexts, while the land–purchase relationship is weaker among urban and wealthier households, suggesting that land ownership may shift households from self-collection to purchase rather than out of biomass use altogether. Time-use regressions further show that land-owning households spend more time gathering and preparing fuel, indicating that access to biomass through land lowers cash expenditures but not labor costs. Overall, the findings suggest that land ownership is an important structural determinant of household fuel use behavior and that cooking transitions may depend not only on income and infrastructure, but also on access to biomass resources through land. The analysis demonstrates that the land–energy nexus deserves greater attention in future household energy research and in policies aimed at accelerating equitable and sustained cooking transitions.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebb4e.title: Additionality of climate benefits from emission reduction and carbon dioxide removal
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebb4e.authors: Ganey, T., Hain, M., Ridgwell, A., Paytan, A.
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebb4e.abstract: Abstract Carbon dioxide removal (CDR) has been identified as a necessary complement to industrial decarbonization for climate change mitigation. Marine CDR (mCDR) approaches, such as ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) and direct ocean capture (DOC), have received considerable attention for their potential to counteract ocean acidification while simultaneously reducing atmospheric CO 2 . However, most model-based assessments of mCDR efficacy either assume a fixed background atmospheric CO 2 value or adopt an idealized future CO 2 trajectory, thereby excluding impacts of important carbon cycle feedbacks that repartition carbon between the ocean, atmosphere, and biosphere. Here, we use an Earth system model to address three core questions: whether the net CO 2 effect of CDR depends on background emissions; whether CDR technologies deployed simultaneously yield additive CO 2 reductions; and whether there is synergy between the radiative forcing (climate) benefits of CDR and emission reductions. We evaluate permutations of direct air capture, OAE, and DOC, quantifying their individual and combined CO 2 effects under various emissions scenarios. We find that the radiative forcing effects of emissions reductions and CDR are largely additive through time, regardless of background emission scenario or CDR type or scale. Furthermore, any given quantity and type of short-term CDR deployment produces a predictable, proportional and durable reduction in atmospheric CO 2 through time (ΔlnCO 2 ), facilitating comparison between CDR strategies. Finally, we show that CDR efficacy is marginally greater at low background CO 2 , supporting the complementary value of decarbonization and CDR in carbon management portfolios. These findings provide a robust physical basis for the design of integrated carbon management strategies and support pursuit of deep emissions cuts and CDR as synergistic climate levers.

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compenvurbsys..title: Have we already lost it? Geoprivacy in the age of AI, uncertainty, and corporate gatekeeping
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compenvurbsys..authors: Milad Malekzadeh, Jim Thatcher, Grant McKenzie et al.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compenvurbsys..abstract: Geoprivacy is often framed as a problem of protecting coordinates, masking traces, or managing user consent. This framing is now insufficient. In an era of pervasive datafication, AI-enabled inference, platform dependence, and corporate control over location and mobility data, the central question is no longer whether exact locations can be hidden, but whether meaningful control over location-derived knowledge remains possible at all. This paper asks: have we already lost geoprivacy? We argue that geoprivacy has not disappeared, but its conditions have fundamentally changed. Location data are now continuously produced through everyday digital participation, linked across platforms and modalities, and transformed by machine learning, large language models, and agentic systems into sensitive inferences about identity, behavior, association, vulnerability, and future action. At the same time, risks and protections are unevenly distributed: privacy increasingly functions as socioeconomic, political, and institutional privilege, while marginalized communities, sensitive places, non-human environments, and collective forms of knowledge face heightened exposure and risk. These challenges are intensified by corporate gateke eping, regulatory lag, harmful defaults, limited transparency, and epistemic blind spots within existing geoprivacy norms and directions. We therefore reposition geoprivacy as a socio-technical, legal, institutional, and political problem, not merely a technical one. Looking forward, we outline responsibilities for policymakers, researchers, communities, and industry, including privacy-protective defaults, regulation of spatial inference, public-good data governance, geoprivacy literacy, cyber-threat exercises, and community-controlled infrastructures. Rather than declaring geoprivacy lost, we argue that it must be continually renegotiated as a moving boundary, one that requires GI science to act not only as a technical field, but as a bridge between spatial reasoning, governance, justice, and democratic control over location-based data and futures.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec17d.title: Global opportunities for climate-resilient coral reef conservation to 2050
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec17d.authors: Kyle J. A. Zawada, Emily S. Darling, Stacy D. Jupiter et al.
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec17d.abstract: Abstract Climate change is accelerating the decline of coral reefs, yet some locations may retain conditions that support persistence under future warming. We compiled 45,064 coral field observations from 1960–2025 and 42 climate, biophysical, and human-pressure predictors to train machine-learning ensembles estimating coral cover and community composition in 2020 and 2050. We then used a multi-objective optimization framework to select, within each ecoregion, 30% of the reef area (consistent with the GBF 30x30 target) that jointly maximized current and future coral cover, community composition, spatial cohesion, and model certainty as indicators of climate resilience. Finally, we evaluated our results against three global coral reef habitat layers, including two products from the Allen Coral Atlas (visible reef extent and a coral habitat subset) and a UNEP-WCMC global distribution of coral reefs. The three layers identify between 36,466 to 167,352 km2 of coral reef areas with relatively high projected persistence to survive climate change, spanning 79 to 81 national EEZs and 57 to 60 territories and jurisdictions. These findings show how empirical observations and multivariate machine learning can be combined to map candidate climate-resilient reefs at fine resolution, and reveal their uneven but widespread global distribution. While predictive skill was modest and varied among provinces, our results identify candidate locations with the highest probability of sustaining functioning coral reef futures rather than definitive priorities, and should be combined with local knowledge, national assessments and improved monitoring data to inform conservation policy, finance and management.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aec169.abstract: Abstract Earth System Models used to quantify climate-carbon cycle feedbacks and remaining carbon budgets are initialised from pre-industrial land-use conditions, yet the real world has experienced centuries of land-use change. Whether the resulting land-surface state affects the diagnosed feedback parameters-concentration-carbon (β land ) and climate-carbon (γ land )-and the Transient Climate Response to cumulative Emissions (TCRE) remains poorly explored.Here we quantify how different initial land-use states-no land-use, pre-industrial, and present-day-affect carbon cycle feedback parameters in standard 1% CO 2 coupled and biogeochemically coupled simulations using HadCM3LC-Bris. Present-day land use reduces β land by 16% and makes γ land 8% more negative relative to no land-use, but the biophysical cooling from deforestation depresses the climate sensitivity parameter α, producing a net 8% reduction in TCRE at 2×CO 2 . This implies a systematic positive bias of ∼8% in TCRE diagnosed from pre-industrial-initialised experiments, corresponding to ∼40 GtCO 2 for a 1.5 • C carbon budget. At higher forcing, the land-use effect on TCRE diminishes as α differences converge while γ land continues to diverge. Our results highlight a baseline-dependent bias in current CMIP protocol design with direct implications for carbon budget estimates.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aeb9fe.title: Reply to Comment on ‘A globally relevant data-driven assessment of carbon leakage from forestry’
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aeb9fe.authors: Daigneault, A., Sohngen, B., Belair, E., Ellis, P.
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aeb9fe.abstract: Abstract Filewod (2026 Environ. Res. Lett. 20 114022) Comment questions whether the Global Timber Model (GTM) used in Daigneault et al (2025 Environ. Res. Lett. 20 114022) should be to quantify the carbon leakage from climate-smart forestry (CSF) practices. We share the Comment’s goal of protecting the integrity of forest carbon credits and mitigate climate change, but differ on whether model-based estimates should inform crediting adjustments, particularly while ex-post evidence of recent CSF projects accumulates. We clarify and stand by our study conclusions that our estimates support ex-ante, multi-factor leakage deductions, that forest carbon leakage can vary widely depending on the project type and location, and that carbon leakage is typically lower than harvest leakage. We also acknowledge the strong market assumptions underlying GTM and show that discounting carbon leakage that accrues in the distant future reduces the influence of far off supply responses thereby providing conservative estimates. We acknowledge that ex-ante model intercomparison and robust ex-post analysis can offer a shared path toward more robust and credible leakage accounting.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebbde.title: Decoupled ore and scrap trade networks constrain low-carbon metal supply
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebbde.authors: Tian, X., Mao, Y., Geng, Y., Taylor, D.
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebbde.abstract: Abstract Global supply chains for critical metals such as aluminium and copper are increasingly exposed to sustainability and geopolitical risks under the pressure of energy transition. In this paper we compare primary (ore) and secondary (scrap) trade networks for the United States, European Union and China using multilayer network analysis. We focus on the years 2010–2023, a period that captures intensified demand for the two metals. Results identify a marked structural decoupling: around 40% of scrap-trading countries do not participate in ore trade. Further, while about 50% of ore trade links overlap with scrap networks, only some 10%–15% of scrap connections overlap with ore trade. Despite strong alignment in trading partners, volumes of scrap and ore trade diverge substantially. The observed differences indicate that the two commodity streams use partly distinct international trading relationships. Major economies may compete for ore suppliers but remain interdependent in scrap trade, revealing a bifurcated system with uneven resilience. Strengthening integration between primary and secondary supply chains is therefore critical for achieving sustainable critical metal supply for the low-carbon energy transition and establishing resource-efficient metal systems.

https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149860.title: Wealth, homeownership, and land use regulatory changes
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149860.authors: Diego Gil, Hugo E. Silva, Kenzo Asahi
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149860.abstract: This paper examines patterns of land use regulatory changes in Santiago, Chile, focusing on downzoning (stricter regulations) and upzoning (more flexible regulations), and their associations with sociodemographic factors. We analyze an original georeferenced dataset covering all 34 urban municipalities of Santiago over 20 years, together with 19 semi-structured interviews with key actors. The quantitative analysis suggests that high-income neighborhoods are associated with a greater likelihood of downzoning when homeownership is comparatively low. With our block-level measure of wealth, however, this association is not statistically distinguishable from zero at the sample-average homeownership rate and becomes negative at higher rates. Therefore, in affluent neighborhoods, the significant presence of homeowners is associated with less probability of downzoning. Outside high-income neighborhoods, higher homeownership is instead associated with downzoning. Qualitative evidence points to the growing role of organized residents, with socially connected groups using participatory reforms and informal ties to municipal decision-makers to shape local regulatory debates. This positive association is absent when the analysis is restricted to large-scale zoning changes. The findings contribute to debates between the “growth machine” and “homevoter” theories by suggesting that the relevance of each framework may vary across patterns of social segmentation and local demographic structures.

https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026150026.title: Activity spaces, community resource brokers, and real-time stress and affect: Evidence from the Boston Activity Space and Health Study
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026150026.abstract: While we know that the places where we live matter for our health and well-being, other spaces in the city we visit during the day—like places where we work, worship, exercise, and buy groceries—also matter. Little work, however, has explored how daily experiences with these routine community institutions and organizations shape our emotional responses. This study uses data from the Boston Activity Space and Health Study (BASHS), a smartphone-based data collection of adults’ GPS locations and ecological momentary assessments, to capture in-the-moment responses to their daily activity space environments for 7 days. We use random effects models to estimate associations between resource broker access and real-time accounts of stress and affect, and whether these relationships are conditional on the utilization of the resource brokers. Our findings suggest that beyond having regular access to community resource brokers, utilizing them on a regular basis is impactful for alleviating momentary emotional and physiological distress. By detailing the unique role of resource brokers, the current study makes substantive and methodological contributions to our understanding of how activity spaces matter for health and well-being.

https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149947.title: Planning for circular urban metabolism: Intertwining skills and spatial transformation for manufacturing transition in Padua and Venice, Italy
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149947.authors: Claudia Faraone, Francesca Gambarotto, Luca Nicoletto, Giulio Pedrini
https://doi.org/10.1177/0042098026149947.abstract: The shift from a linear to a circular economic structure needs a new urban metabolism that minimizes waste and the use of raw materials and energy. However, a city’s potential for circularity is contingent upon its manufacturing path-dependency, both from an economic and spatial perspective. The research looks at two Italian industrial areas—Padua and Venice—and proceeds to investigate the recent dynamics of their manufacturing spatial distribution at the “transect” level scale. Using a mixed-method approach that combines morphological-spatial analysis, urban planning assessment, and quantitative labor and waste data, the study investigates how manufacturing industries contribute to circular transitions and how planning policies can support or hinder this process. Findings show that technological manufacturing, supported by technical skills and green jobs, drives circular performance through waste prevention and recycling. Industrial diversification and firm relatedness further enable symbiotic material flows. However, both cities reveal a persistent misalignment between emerging circular dynamics and existing zoning frameworks. While Padua has begun adopting mixed-use zoning, planning strategies in both areas remain fragmented and reactive. The paper calls for more integrated, circularity-oriented spatial planning that mobilizes skills and proximity as key territorial resources.

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.1.title: From emissions to damage: A mechanism-based assessment of artificial intelligence's environmental cost and the limits of the sustainable energy transition
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.1.authors: Ramez Abubakr Badeeb
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.1.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming the global economy, but its environmental impact presents a clear paradox, as it can improve efficiency while also increasing energy demand. Existing studies focus mainly on emissions, while policymakers care about the associated welfare losses. This paper shifts the analysis from emissions to carbon damage, capturing the monetized cost imposed on economies and societies. It also investigates and quantifies the mediating role of sustainable energy transition in the relationship between artificial intelligence and carbon damage. Using panel data from 37 OECD countries and employing instrumental variable two-step GMM estimation supported by three robustness checks, our results reveal three findings. First, AI significantly increases carbon damage, confirming that AI's scale and energy demand outweigh efficiency gains. Second, AI significantly promotes sustainable energy transition measured through a newly developed composite index capturing renewable deployment, energy access, and efficiency. This reveals the presence of a beneficial indirect channel. Third, the Sobel mediation analysis confirms that this channel offsets a limited share of AI's total carbon damage. Across our estimators, the implied mediation share remains below 15%, indicating that the self-correcting capacity of the sustainable energy transition is real but quantitatively limited. Moreover, a suppression mediation pattern is additionally identified, revealing that studies relying on total effect estimation without mediation decomposition underestimate AI's true direct environmental cost. This finding moves the debate beyond the question of whether AI is good or bad for the environment toward the more policy-relevant question of how much of AI's environmental cost the sustainable energy transition can absorb.

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.1.title: Trade-offs between greenhouse gas mitigation and nutrient enrichment during tropical composting
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.1.authors: Edwin Mwangi, Felix K. Ngetich, Collins Muimi Musafiri et al.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.1.abstract: Composting provides an opportunity to recycle organic residues into valuable soil amendments; however, amendment selection can create trade-offs between nutrient enrichment and greenhouse gas (GHG) mitigation. Our study evaluated the effects of different organic amendment combinations on GHG emissions and nutrient dynamics during tropical composting. Six cattle manure-based treatments were assessed: cattle manure alone (CM), cattle manure with Tithonia diversifolia (CMT), Tithonia with biochar (CMTB), Tithonia with citric acid (CMTCA), Tithonia with maize stover (CMTM), and Tithonia, maize stover, and citric acid (CMTMCA). We monitored composting for 84 days, measuring CO 2 , CH 4 , and N 2 O emissions alongside changes in temperature, moisture, pH, and carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus fractions. Greenhouse gas emissions concentrated during the thermophilic phase, the period of greatest emission intensity due to enhanced substrate availability, rapid carbon mineralization, and active microbial transformation. During this phase, cumulative CH 4 emissions ranged from 299 to 1284 g CH 4 –C m −2 , with CMTCA producing 180% higher emissions than CM, while cumulative CO 2 emissions ranged from 10.8 to 14.1 kg CO 2 –C m −2 , with CMTMCA and CMTCA producing 23% and 13% higher emissions than CM, respectively. CMTCA produced the greatest cumulative CH 4 emissions, exceeding CM by 165%. This response reflects the combined influence of Tithonia diversifolia and citric acid addition, where enhanced carbon solubilization increased substrate availability and microbial oxygen demand, potentially promoting transient anaerobic microsites favorable for methane production. Across the composting period, CMTM generated the highest cumulative CO 2 emissions, 18.5% higher than CM, reflecting enhanced carbon turnover from readily degradable substrates in Tithonia diversifolia and maize stover. Biochar amendment (CMTB) increased cumulative N 2 O emissions by 41% compared with CM, suggesting that biochar effects were dependent on interactions with nitrogen-rich Tithonia and compost nitrogen transformation pathways. Conversely, Tithonia-based amendments improved nitrogen enrichment but increased emission risks. Overall, the findings demonstrate that climate-smart composting requires balancing nutrient recovery and GHG mitigation rather than optimising either outcome in isolation. For smallholder farmers in tropical regions, the findings demonstrate that locally available organic amendments can improve compost nutrient characteristics. However, amendment selection should consider potential trade-offs between nutrient enrichment and greenhouse gas emissions.

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.1.authors: John Kwame Bediako, Mohammadamin Esmaeili, Godfred Ohemeng‐Boahen et al.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.1.abstract: The use of waste materials as low-cost adsorbents for treating water pollutants offers many advantages as they contribute to reducing waste disposal costs and aiding sustainable resource management. Synthetic textile wastes pose environmental threats, hence their upcycling to adsorbents for treating water pollutants presents a good option for sustainability and circularity. The synthetic textiles are employed in their pristine, chemically functionalized, or morphologically tailored forms, including fiber felts, electrospun membranes, 3D-printed monoliths, and activated carbon (AC). This review critically examined up-to-date research, common target pollutants, performance and trends regarding the upcycling of synthetic textiles to produce functional adsorbents for water treatment. Generally, adsorption performance towards organic and inorganic pollutants including emerging contaminants is controlled by surface area/porosity, surface functionality/chemistry, morphology, crystallinity, wettability, and stability. For metals and dyes, performance depends almost entirely on functionalization, e.g., coatings, grafting, carbonization. For hydrocarbons and oils, hydrophobic pristine textiles already perform well, however, performance is further improved via surface functionalization. For emerging contaminants such as microplastics and PFAS, synthetic textiles are largely underutilized, with current evidence dominated by microplastic-vector studies and composite materials rather than purpose-designed textile-based adsorbents. Noteworthily, the upcycled adsorbents serve potentially lower-cost and more circular alternatives in location-specific applications, rather than universal replacements for AC or ion exchange resins. Consequently, synthetic textile-derived adsorbents are economically promising, however, rigorous cost analysis, regeneration, real wastewater systems, and scale-up operations remain a major missing piece and a clear priority for future research. Additionally, comprehensive leaching and chemical screening are required prior to deployment. Moreover, spent adsorbents and regeneration liquors must be managed through metal recovery, eluate treatment, or controlled destruction, consistent with for example, EU textile collection and EPR policies. Standardized testing should quantify hydraulic performance, breakthrough behavior, dynamic capacity, mass transfer, mechanical stability, material shedding, bed utilization, and regeneration durability to enable reliable adsorbent comparisons.

https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebdaa.title: Spatio-temporal dynamics of migrating wet and dry extremes: structural coherence and land-use associations across India
https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aebdaa.abstract: Abstract Global hydroclimatic extremes increasingly occur as cascading wet–dry sequences, challenging conventional single-hazard management. However, their spatiotemporal migration and associations with land-use patterns remain poorly understood. We present an integrated framework combining the standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index, a spatio-temporal density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise algorithm, and phase-wise land-use/land-cover (LULC) exposure analysis to characterize the migration, structural coherence, and persistence of major wet and dry extremes across India. Both dry and wet events exhibit a range of migration directions rather than a single dominant pathway, spanning northward, southward, and eastward trajectories. Although several recent events are among the least coherent, a linear-trend test does not establish a temporal shift towards fragmentation ( p = 0.74 for dry and p = 0.16 for wet events). A pronounced asymmetry between rapid onset and a prolonged recovery phase (2–3 months) highlights the persistence of hydroclimatic extremes. Phase-wise LULC analysis indicates that agricultural landscapes show the greatest absolute exposure, largely reflecting their extensive national footprint, while urban areas are frequently associated with recovery-stage wet events. The proposed framework provides a transferable approach for improving early-warning systems and supporting land-use-informed adaptation to compound hydroclimatic hazards.
