https://doi.org/10.1111/disa.70083.title: Lived experiences of people affected by the 2024 spring flood disaster in Kazakhstan: a phenomenological study
https://doi.org/10.1111/disa.70083.authors: Dias Baiseitov, Jonas Preposi Cruz, Ejercito Mangawa Balay‐odao
https://doi.org/10.1111/disa.70083.abstract: This study describes the lived experiences of people affected by the 2024 spring flood disaster in the Republic of Kazakhstan. It utilises a descriptive phenomenological qualitative research design and Canadian scholar Max Van Manen's data analysis approach. The pool of participants comprises 13 individuals who experienced flooding in the country's Aktobe Region, pinpointed through referral sampling. Semi-structured interviews were used to collect the data and the researchers ensured rigour and trustworthiness throughout the project. Initially, 183 codes were identified in the analysis. These were then summarised by meaning, yielding 13 subthemes that were further categorised into four themes: (i) Disrupted Lifeworld: Displacement, Loss, and Disruption of Everyday Life; (ii) Emotional and Existential Consequences of Disaster and Displacement; (iii) Experiencing Social and Institutional Relationships During Recovery; and (iv) Reconstructing Life: Coping, Agency, and Adaptation. The study underscores the need to refine disaster response mechanisms from multiple perspectives, encompassing personal resilience and more effective policies. The disaster in Kazakhstan affected people's intrapersonal relationships and their mental and material well-being.

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compenvurbsys..title: Hidden and fragmented patterns of morphological informality across African cities revealed by open geospatial data
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compenvurbsys..authors: Wenbin Zhang, Weixuan Fang, Alessandro Sorichetta et al.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compenvurbsys..abstract: Informal settlements are a major yet poorly measured form of urbanization, particularly where small or fragmented clusters are embedded within otherwise formal urban fabric. Here, we develop a scalable geospatial framework for mapping morphological informality across African cities using open satellite imagery, global building data, and eight city-specific machine-learning models combined by equal averaging. Applied to all 84 African cities with projected populations exceeding one million in 2025, the framework generates 10 m probability surfaces. Mean leave-one-city-out F1 at training-selected thresholds was 0.876; independent validation using 1910 reference points yielded AUC of 0.972. Building-presence profiles were the leading SHAP contributor in all eight held-out cities, with height and spectral context providing additional signals. These results support retaining neighborhood building distributions alongside vertical structure and vegetation when mapping across diverse urban contexts. The share of selected area in patches smaller than 1 km 2 increased from 38.0% at p ≥ 0.2 to 72.4% at p ≥ 0.8. WorldPop 2023 allocated fewer people than community-reported counts in 89.0% of 308 settlement polygons, with a median WorldPop/community ratio of 0.263. Community records span 2013–2020, so the comparison diagnoses allocation discrepancies and motivates assessing settlement-specific population densities using contemporaneous evidence. The probability surfaces describe physical morphology, not tenure or household deprivation. Together, the findings identify shared morphological signals and population-allocation discrepancies that can guide local validation, surveys and future population modelling.

https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-026-04338.title: Climate change adaptation in the Philippines: a systematic review of empirical evidence
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-026-04338.authors: Henry Antoine Bartelet, Luisa Fernanda Bedoya Taborda
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-026-04338.abstract: Highly climate-vulnerable countries face the dual challenge of responding to growing climate hazards while addressing the social and institutional conditions that shape vulnerability and adaptation. National evidence syntheses are needed to assess how adaptation research is progressing and whether it provides evidence about the outcomes of adaptation responses. We examine these questions in the Philippines, where climate exposure intersects with livelihood precarity, social vulnerability, and uneven institutional capacity. We conducted a systematic review of empirical evidence on human climate change adaptation in the Philippines and identified 99 relevant studies published between 2010 and 2024. We analysed their research themes and empirical findings, together with the subset directly assessing adaptation outcomes or effectiveness. The literature predominantly examines perceptions, adaptive capacity, and sectoral responses, particularly in fisheries, coastal settings, and agriculture. Over time, research has broadened from local vulnerability, coastal risk, and household coping toward institutional capacity, managed retreat, social capital, justice, and equity. However, only 13 studies directly evaluated adaptation outcomes. These studies found that adaptation can improve yields, food security, housing, safety, and local resilience, but that benefits depend on markets, technical support, institutional capacity, and fair implementation. Adaptation responses can also produce ecological degradation, livelihood disruption, and unequal access to benefits. Philippine adaptation research therefore has a substantial descriptive and diagnostic evidence base but a much smaller evaluative one. More integrated research is needed to connect adaptive capacities and barriers to the responses they enable or constrain, the outcomes these responses produce, and subsequent feedbacks to future adaptive capacity.

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.autcon.2026.10.title: Bridging scan-to-BIM and facility management: an IFC-driven framework for information automation in existing buildings
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.autcon.2026.10.authors: Zicheng Zhu, Kun Tian, Matthew Moorhead, Martin Skitmore
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.autcon.2026.10.abstract: Facility management (FM) of existing buildings is hindered by fragmented records and Scan-to-BIM models that remain difficult to reuse in operations. This paper presents an IFC-driven framework that transforms four discipline-specific Scan-to-BIM models into a lightweight FM knowledge base and a web-based digital building management system (WDBMS). The framework extracts assets, spaces, storeys, systems, properties, spatial containment, system membership, and MEP port connectivity; normalises them into an FM schema; evaluates information readiness through configurable requirements; and preserves IFC relationship and source-file provenance. Parallel geometry preprocessing produces lightweight web meshes linked to records. The WDBMS integrates a BIM Viewer, Data Workspace, and Knowledge Graph to support bidirectional asset retrieval, validation review, provenance inspection, and topology tracing. The case generated 5345 assets, 90 spaces, 22 storeys, 199 systems, 8091 typed relationships, and 2051 physical connections. This reproducible post-IFC process makes multidisciplinary Scan-to-BIM deliverables queryable, auditable, and operationally accessible.

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.autcon.2026.10.title: Topology-driven automated generation of geometric digital twins for railway overhead line equipment
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.autcon.2026.10.authors: M.R. Mahendrini Fernando Ariyachandra, Ioannis Brilakis
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.autcon.2026.10.abstract: Generating geometric digital twins (GDTs) of railway overhead line equipment (OLE) from point cloud data (PCD) using manual or semi-automated approaches is labour-intensive. This diminishes their practical benefits, with 74% of modelling effort spent converting PCD into GDTs. Automation reduces cost and effort, yet state-of-the-art methods struggle to deliver kilometre-scale GDTs without precision loss or manual intervention. This paper presents an automated method combining topology-aware segmentation, rule-based classification, and template-driven geometric reconstruction. Leveraging engineering rules and OLE spatial relationships, it enables modelling in cluttered, partially occluded scenes. OLE elements are segmented into labelled clusters, then aligned with parametric assemblies to generate industry foundation classes (IFC) models. Evaluation on 18.5 km of PCD achieved F1 scores of 98.3% for C sections, 89.8% for contact and 84.1% for catenary cables, with ±5.6 cm RMSE. Automation saved 98.6% of time versus manual workflows.
